title: What are the different ways to create a `String` (literal → pooled, `new String(...)` → heap object, from `char[]`, from `byte[]` + `Charset`), and how do they differ in memory and `==` behavior?
shortTitle: What are the different ways to create a String?

s1_definition.profdef: A String can be created as a literal, which the JVM places in the string pool and reuses so equal literals share one object; with `new String(...)`, which always allocates a fresh object on the heap distinct from the pooled copy; from a `char[]` via a constructor that copies the characters into a new heap String; and from a `byte[]` together with a `Charset`, which decodes the raw bytes into characters using the given encoding. These differ in memory because pooled literals are shared while `new` and array-based constructions create separate objects, and they differ in reference comparison because two literals of the same content are `==` equal, whereas a `new` String is a different object and is not `==` equal to the pooled literal even when the contents match.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the word "SETTLED" that appears on thousands of forms at National Bank of India. A string literal is like a single official rubber stamp kept in a shared drawer: everyone who needs "SETTLED" uses the same stamp, so it is one physical object reused everywhere. Using new String is like photocopying that stamp onto a brand-new separate card every time, so even though the word reads the same, it is a different physical card. Building from a character array is like assembling the word letter by letter onto a new card. Building from raw bytes plus a charset is like receiving the word in a coded telegram and decoding it with a specific codebook onto a new card. The shared stamp equals itself by identity, but a photocopy is a different card even though the words match.
s1_definition.oneliner: Literals are pooled and shared so equal literals are == equal; new String, char[], and byte[]-with-charset all create distinct heap objects that are equals-equal but not ==-equal to the pooled literal.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A String can be created as a literal, which the JVM places in the string pool and reuses so equal literals share one object; with `new String(...)`, which always allocates a fresh object on the heap distinct from the pooled copy; from a `char[]` via a constructor that copies the characters into a new heap String; and from a `byte[]` together with a `Charset`, which decodes the raw bytes into characters using the given encoding. These differ in memory because pooled literals are shared while `new` and array-based constructions create separate objects, and they differ in reference comparison because two literals of the same content are `==` equal, whereas a `new` String is a different object and is not `==` equal to the pooled literal even when the contents match.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the word "SETTLED" that appears on thousands of forms at National Bank of India. A string literal is like a single official rubber stamp kept in a shared drawer: everyone who needs "SETTLED" uses the same stamp, so it is one physical object reused everywhere. Using new String is like photocopying that stamp onto a brand-new separate card every time, so even though the word reads the same, it is a different physical card. Building from a character array is like assembling the word letter by letter onto a new card. Building from raw bytes plus a charset is like receiving the word in a coded telegram and decoding it with a specific codebook onto a new card. The shared stamp equals itself by identity, but a photocopy is a different card even though the words match.

**One line to remember:** Literals are pooled and shared so equal literals are == equal; new String, char[], and byte[]-with-charset all create distinct heap objects that are equals-equal but not ==-equal to the pooled literal.

sections.s2_technical:
A String literal written in source code, such as "SETTLED", is handled specially by the compiler and class loader. All literals of identical content are interned into the string pool, which in modern JVMs lives in the regular heap, and they share a single String object. So if two variables are both assigned the literal "SETTLED", they point at the same object, and comparing them with the double-equals reference operator returns true. This sharing saves memory because the same text used in many places costs only one object. The pool is why literals are the most efficient way to express constant strings.

Using the new String constructor always allocates a brand-new String object on the heap, separate from any pooled copy. If you write new String("SETTLED"), you actually create two things: the pooled literal "SETTLED" that the constructor argument refers to, and a second, distinct heap object that copies that content. The variable points at the fresh object, not the pooled one, so comparing it with double-equals against the literal returns false, because they are different objects, even though equals returns true because the contents match. This is why new String is almost always wasteful and discouraged for plain text: it needlessly creates a second object and breaks the convenient reference equality of literals. You can recover the pooled instance by calling intern on the new String, which returns the canonical pooled object.

Creating a String from a char array uses a constructor that copies the characters into a new String's internal storage. For example new String(new char[]{'S','E','T'}) builds a fresh heap String whose content is the array's characters. This is a distinct object, not pooled, so it is not double-equals equal to any literal. A related point is that building from a char array copies the data defensively, so later changes to the array do not affect the String, preserving String immutability. Char arrays are also used when handling sensitive data like passwords, because unlike a String they can be zeroed out after use, though that is a security nuance rather than a pooling one.

Creating a String from a byte array plus a Charset decodes raw bytes into characters using the specified encoding, as in new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8). This is essential when reading data from files, network sockets, or databases, where you receive bytes and must interpret them as text under a known encoding. The critical rule is to always specify the Charset explicitly, because the no-charset constructor uses the platform default encoding, which varies by environment and causes subtle corruption of non-ASCII characters, a classic production bug in international banking data. The resulting String is again a distinct heap object, not pooled.

The memory and reference-comparison summary is the heart of the question. Literals are shared in the pool, so equal literals are double-equals equal. Every other construction, new String, char array, and byte array with charset, produces a separate heap object that is equals-equal in content but not double-equals equal to the pooled literal or to each other. The senior rule that follows is that you compare String content with equals, never with double-equals, precisely because only pooled literals share identity and any string built at runtime will not. You use literals for constants, you avoid new String for plain text, you always specify a charset when decoding bytes, and you reserve intern for deliberate canonicalization in hot paths.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India routes transactions by a status word. A developer compared a status built at runtime from incoming bytes against the literal "SETTLED" using the double-equals operator, and the comparison failed even though the text matched, so transactions were misrouted. This is exactly the pooling and reference-equality behaviour: the runtime-built String is a separate heap object and is not double-equals equal to the pooled literal.

Problem 2 — The ingestion layer read status bytes from a network feed without specifying a charset, and non-ASCII remarks were corrupted on some servers. This is exactly the byte-array-plus-charset rule: you must decode with an explicit Charset, not the platform default.

Problem 3 — The team needs to understand when strings are shared and when they are distinct, to compare correctly with equals and to avoid wasteful new String usage. This is exactly the memory-and-identity picture across literal, new, char array, and byte array constructions.

We will build a runnable demo that creates the same content four ways, prints the reference-equality and content-equality results, shows the charset decoding of bytes, demonstrates intern recovering the pooled object, and shows correct status routing with equals. The code includes a StatusComparator and a demo main.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the content "SETTLED" created four different ways.

Step 1: Two literal assignments both reference the single pooled "SETTLED" object, so comparing them with the reference operator returns true. This shows literals are shared in the pool.

Step 2: The new String constructor copies the content into a fresh heap object. Comparing it with the literal using the reference operator returns false because they are different objects, while equals returns true because the contents match.

Step 3: Building from a character array copies the characters into another new heap object. Again the reference comparison with the literal is false and the content comparison is true, confirming it is a distinct object.

Step 4: Encoding the text to UTF-8 bytes and decoding it back with the explicit UTF-8 charset produces yet another distinct heap object. The reference comparison is false, equals is true, and crucially the explicit charset guarantees the bytes are decoded correctly regardless of the server's default encoding.

Step 5: Calling intern on the new String returns the canonical pooled object, so comparing that interned result with the literal using the reference operator returns true, showing how to recover identity when you deliberately want it.

Step 6: The routing demonstration shows the bug and the fix: comparing the runtime-built status to the literal with the reference operator returns false and misroutes, while comparing with equals returns true and routes correctly, proving you must compare string content with equals.

```
2026-10-30 18:11:30 INFO    literal1 == literal2 ? true (shared pool object)
2026-10-30 18:11:30 INFO    viaNew == literal1 ? false (different object) ; equals ? true
2026-10-30 18:11:30 INFO    viaChars == literal1 ? false ; equals ? true
2026-10-30 18:11:30 INFO    viaBytes == literal1 ? false ; equals ? true
2026-10-30 18:11:30 INFO    viaNew.intern() == literal1 ? true (canonical)
2026-10-30 18:11:30 WARNING Routing by == on runtime string: false (BUG — misroutes!)
2026-10-30 18:11:30 INFO    Routing by equals on runtime string: true (CORRECT)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  content "SETTLED" created four ways
    │
    ├─ "SETTLED" literal ───┐
    │  "SETTLED" literal ───┼→ SAME pooled object  → == true
    │
    ├─ new String("SETTLED") → NEW heap object #1  → == false, equals true
    ├─ new String(char[])    → NEW heap object #2  → == false, equals true
    └─ new String(bytes,UTF8)→ NEW heap object #3  → == false, equals true
                                      │ intern()
                                      ▼
                               returns pooled object → == true

  Rule: compare with equals(), never ==, for string CONTENT.
  Rule: decoding bytes → ALWAYS pass an explicit Charset.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — String Creation & Identity ═══

  ┌─ Rules ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ literal        → pooled, shared, == equal to equal lit  │
  │ new String     → new heap object, != literal            │
  │ char[]         → new heap object (defensive copy)       │
  │ byte[]+Charset → new heap object (decode; specify CS!)  │
  │ intern()       → returns canonical pooled object        │
  │ compare CONTENT → equals(), never ==                    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID / Rules ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Comparator routes; demo constructs                   │
  │ Rule: literals for constants; avoid new String for text │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Memory view ──────────────────────────────────────────
  String Pool:   ["SETTLED"] ← literal1, literal2, interned
  Heap:          obj#1(new), obj#2(char[]), obj#3(bytes)
                 each distinct; equals==true, ==false vs pool

  Contract for new String(byte[], Charset):
    Pre:  charset matches the producer's encoding
    Post: new heap String decoded correctly
    Caution: omitting charset uses platform default → corruption
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
There are four main ways to create a String, and they differ in both memory and reference behaviour. A literal written in source code is interned into the string pool, which lives in the heap, and all literals of identical content share one object, so two variables assigned the same literal are reference-equal under the double-equals operator. This sharing is efficient and is why literals are the right way to express constant strings. Using the new String constructor always allocates a fresh, distinct object on the heap, separate from the pooled copy, so a new String is not reference-equal to the literal even though the contents match, which makes new String wasteful for plain text and is why it is discouraged. Building from a character array copies the characters into another distinct heap object, defensively so later array changes do not affect the String. Building from a byte array together with a Charset decodes raw bytes into characters using the given encoding and also produces a distinct heap object.

The memory picture is that literals are shared in the pool while every other construction creates a separate object, and the reference picture follows directly: equal literals are double-equals equal, but a new String, a char-array String, and a byte-array String are each a different object, equals-equal in content but not double-equals equal to the pooled literal or to each other. You can recover the pooled canonical instance by calling intern, which returns the shared object. The practical rule that follows is that you always compare string content with equals and never with the double-equals operator, precisely because only pooled literals share identity and anything built at runtime will not.

In a project at National Bank of India this caused a real bug. A developer compared an incoming status, built at runtime from network bytes, against the literal using the double-equals operator, and the comparison failed even though the text was "SETTLED", so transactions were misrouted. The fix was simply to compare with equals, which looks at content. We hit a second classic bug in the same path when the bytes were decoded without specifying a charset, so non-ASCII remarks were corrupted on servers whose platform default encoding differed, and we fixed that by always decoding with an explicit UTF-8 Charset.

So the principles I always state are these. Use literals for constant strings because they are pooled and shared. Avoid new String for plain text because it needlessly creates a second object and breaks the convenient identity of literals. When building from a character array, remember it is a distinct object that defensively copies the data. When decoding a byte array into text, always pass an explicit Charset rather than relying on the platform default, which is a frequent source of corruption in international data. Compare string content with equals, never with the double-equals operator, and reserve intern for deliberate canonicalization in hot paths where you genuinely want reference equality. That covers how each construction behaves in memory and under reference comparison, and why it matters in production.

---

keyPoints: Literal: abc — goes to String Pool, reused
new String(abc) — new heap object, not pooled
From byte[] + Charset: new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
Always specify Charset explicitly — platform default is not portable
